title: Penalties for a Holy People
summary: This chapter attaches penalties to many of the practices forbidden in chapters 18 and 19: giving children to Molech, consulting mediums, cursing parents, adultery, incest, sexual relations between men, and bestiality. Some offenses carry death at the hands of the community, others the threat that God himself will cut the offender off or leave him childless. Between the laws God repeats his call to holiness: he has set Israel apart from the nations to be his own.
story: Chapter 18 laid out forbidden sexual relationships as a list of principles addressed to "you". Chapter 19 described the positive shape of a holy life. Chapter 20 now answers the question every law code must answer: what happens when these commands are broken? It is the enforcement chapter of the Holiness Code, and its tone is sterner. Yet it is not only a penal code. It begins and ends with the danger of turning to other spiritual powers (Molech and mediums) and returns twice to God's purpose, that Israel be holy because he is holy. The next chapters (21 and 22) move to the special holiness required of priests.
historical:
Like its neighbors, Israel lived under laws that prescribed death for serious crimes. The Code of Hammurabi, for example, prescribed death for adultery, though it allowed the husband to spare his wife, in which case the king could spare the man. Leviticus 20 differs in the offenses it counts most serious. It places the offering of children to Molech first, and it treats sins against parents and against the family's sexual boundaries as crimes against God, not only against a household.

How often these penalties were carried out in ancient Israel is not clear. The historical books record the stoning of Achan (Joshua 7) and of Naboth on false charges (1 Kings 21), but they also record adulterers, including King David, who were not executed. By the time of the Mishnah, around AD 200, the rabbis had surrounded capital cases with so many procedural safeguards that execution was rare. The Mishnah (Makkot 1:10) records a view that a court which executed one person in seven years was called destructive. Ahaz and Manasseh, kings of Judah who made their sons pass through the fire (2 Kings 16:3 and 21:6), a practice 2 Kings 23:10 links with Molech, were never punished under this law by their people, and the prophets treated the practice as one of the sins that brought on exile.
cultural:
The chapter assumes a community in which enforcement was shared. "The people of the land" (verse 2) were the free landowning citizens, and stoning was carried out by them together, which made the whole community responsible. Verses 4 and 5 warn that if the community looks the other way, God will act against the offender and his family himself. The repeated formula "their blood is upon them" meant that those carrying out the sentence did not incur bloodguilt: the guilty had brought their death on themselves.

The penalties are graded. Some offenses carry death by the community. Others are left to God, who will cut the offender off (verses 3, 5, 6, 17, 18), or will leave the couple childless (verses 20 and 21), a fitting punishment for sins that confused family lines. The burning in verse 14 may refer to burning the body after execution, as Achan's family and possessions were burned after stoning (Joshua 7:25), but interpreters differ. The ban on marrying a brother's wife in verse 21 was generally understood to apply while the brother lived or had children; Deuteronomy 25:5-10 required a man to marry his brother's childless widow to continue his brother's name.
literary: Unlike chapter 18, which speaks directly ("You must not"), chapter 20 is written mostly in case law: "If a man" does something, then a penalty follows. Many scholars see a deliberate frame. The laws on Molech and mediums (verses 2 to 6) are balanced by the law on mediums at the end (verse 27), and the calls to holiness in verses 7 and 8 are balanced by verses 22 to 26. Between them the laws run roughly from the most serious penalties to the lighter ones. The phrase translated "must surely be put to death" repeats a Hebrew verb twice for emphasis, a standard form in biblical law. The chapter ties its call to holiness to the food laws of chapter 11: Israel is to distinguish clean from unclean animals because God has distinguished Israel from the nations (verses 24 to 26).

outline.t: Molech and mediums: turning to other powers
Offenses punished by being cut off or left childless
Set apart from the nations to be God's own

doctrines.note: God both commands holiness (be holy, verse 7) and gives it (I am the LORD who sanctifies you, verse 8). Israel's holiness is first God's act of setting them apart, and then their life of living up to what he has made them.

The chapter treats sin as serious enough to cost a life. Its penalties express the conviction that some acts destroy the community's life before God, and that God himself will judge those whom human courts fail to punish.

The chapter opens and closes with the worship of Molech and the consulting of the dead. The language of prostitution (verses 5 and 6) presents these as betrayal of the God to whom Israel belongs, not merely as religious error.

The law here functions as a civil code for Israel as a nation under God. Christians have generally distinguished between the moral wrongs it names and the penalties it assigns within Israel's theocracy.

words.note: Mut, to die. It appears twenty times in this chapter, most often in the doubled form mot yumat, translated "must surely be put to death". The doubling gives the sentence force and finality, and the same form appears for murder in Exodus 21:12.
Dam, blood. The refrain their blood is upon them uses blood to mean guilt for a death. It declares that the responsibility belongs to the offender, not to the community that carries out the sentence.

Qadash, to consecrate or make holy. In verse 7 it is Israel's duty (consecrate yourselves), and in verse 8 it is God's act (the LORD who sanctifies you). The two belong together: the people are to become in practice what God has already declared them to be.

Badal, to separate or distinguish. It appears in verses 24, 25, and 26. The same verb describes God separating light from darkness and the waters in Genesis 1. Israel's distinctions between clean and unclean animals mirror God's distinction of Israel from the nations.

christ: The New Testament does not carry these penalties into the church. When Paul confronts a case of incest in Corinth, he quotes Deuteronomy's formula "Expel the wicked man from among you" (1 Corinthians 5:13) but applies it through church discipline, removal from fellowship, not execution. In John 8, a passage many early manuscripts lack but which the church has long treasured, Jesus is confronted with a woman caught in adultery and says, "Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her" (John 8:7), then sends her away with "Now go and sin no more" (John 8:11). He neither denies her sin nor enforces the penalty. Paul's verdict that "the wages of sin is death" (Romans 6:23) echoes the seriousness of this chapter, and the gospel's answer is that Christ bore that death himself. Verse 26, where God sets Israel apart to be his own, is echoed in 1 Peter 2:9, which calls the church "a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession".

hard.q: How should readers understand laws that prescribe death for adultery, cursing parents, and sexual sins?
hard.a: The penalties are severe by any modern standard, and it is honest to say so. Several responses are offered. Many interpreters stress that these laws were given to Israel as a nation under God's direct rule, where the community's purity was tied to God's presence in its midst, and that they were never meant as a template for other nations. Some scholars note that Numbers 35:31 forbids accepting a ransom only for a murderer, which may imply that other capital sentences could be commuted by payment, so that the death penalty marked the gravity of the offense rather than a mandatory sentence in every case. Jewish tradition developed rules of evidence that made executions very rare. Christians have generally held that the moral wrongs named here remain wrong, while the penalties belonged to Israel's civil law and are not carried into the church, which disciplines by exclusion and restoration rather than death. Some Christian thinkers, a minority, have argued that these civil penalties should still guide modern law. On any reading, the chapter asks readers to take seriously that God considers these acts deadly to a community's life.

questions: The chapter warns that if the community ignores a serious wrong, God holds the community accountable too. When have you seen a group protect wrongdoing by looking away?
Verse 8 says God is the one who sanctifies, and verse 7 commands the people to consecrate themselves. How do God's work and our effort fit together in growing in holiness?
Jesus neither excused the woman in John 8 nor condemned her. What would it look like to take sin as seriously as this chapter does while extending mercy as he did?
